Q2 cross-joins Frequents with itself, then groups by the two drinker names; the HAVING compares SUM(f1.times_a_week) to SUM(f2.times_a_week). Because of the cross join, these sums scale by the counts of rows per drinker: for drinkers A (m rows, sumA) and B (n rows, sumB), Q2 checks n*sumA = m*sumB, not sumA = sumB. Q2 also includes self-pairs (A,A), which always satisfy the HAVING, while Q1 excludes them via f1.drinker < f2.drinker. Hence they are not equivalent.
counterexample_dsp: Use a database with only one drinker who frequents at least one bar. Q1 returns no rows because it requires two distinct drinkers (f1.drinker < f2.drinker). Q2 returns the self-pair (A,A) since the HAVING clause holds trivially for the same drinker (the cross-join/grouping makes both sums equal).
